analysis.one_liner: Repeals the law shielding gun makers and dealers from most civil lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 142 House members including its sponsor, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act blocks most lawsuits against gun and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, and dealers for harm caused by the criminal misuse of a firearm. This bill would repeal that shield, letting victims sue the industry in state and federal court like they can sue other product makers. It would also make federal gun-trace data usable as evidence in civil cases, instead of keeping it off-limits.
analysis.who_benefits: Victims of gun violence and their families, who currently cannot hold manufacturers or dealers accountable in court even when trace evidence suggests negligent or unlawful distribution. Plaintiffs' lawyers and state courts gain a new docket of product-liability cases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun violence victims and their families

how_it_helps.text: Repeals sections 2 through 4 of the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, which currently prohibits civil actions against firearm or ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, and trade associations for damages from the criminal or unlawful misuse of a firearm.

Allows firearms trace data held by the ATF's National Trace Center to be subpoenaed, admitted as evidence, and used in civil actions or administrative proceedings, on the same basis as other information.

analysis.who_pays: Gun and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, and their trade associations, who would face civil suits and discovery that current law blocks them from. Some litigation costs could ultimately reach consumers through prices or insurance.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations

drawbacks.text: The bill would restore the ability to sue firearm makers and sellers for damages resulting from the criminal or unlawful misuse of a firearm, meaning businesses could face lawsuits over crimes committed with lawfully sold products by third parties they did not control.

Reopening liability for a lawful product could raise litigation and insurance costs for small gun dealers, not just large manufacturers, and defenders of the current law argue that was the reason Congress enacted the shield in 2005.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: victims get the same right to sue that exists for nearly every other consumer product, while the gun industry loses a legal shield no other industry enjoys and faces the ordinary costs and risks of civil litigation. The objection that sellers could be blamed for third-party crimes is real, but it is the standard risk every other product maker already bears, and courts would still have to prove the sellers did something wrong. The bill died without a vote, so neither the benefit nor the cost was ever tested.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee took no further action on it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Schiff introduced the bill in the House on June 15, 2023, with 51 original cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary on June 15, 2023, which was its only action beyond introduction.
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any further action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

The bill would have repealed the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, which blocks civil suits against the gun industry for damages from criminal or unlawful misuse of firearms, and would have made ATF trace data discoverable in civil cases.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers, sellers, and trade associations keep the legal immunity the bill would have repealed, and no lawsuit liability or trace-data discovery was opened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun manufacturers and sellers, who keep their legal shield

for.name: Adam Schiff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the gun industry's civil liability shield and make trace data usable in court.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no further action — no markup, no vote, no report — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for consideration.

against.name: Gun industry and allied groups such as the National Rifle Association
against.role: Beneficiaries of the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act
against.what_they_did: Long opposed repealing the liability shield and pressed Congress to keep it in place.

sides.party_line_note: All 142 supporters were Democrats — the sponsor plus 141 of 216 House Democrats — with no Republican cosponsors, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Gun and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, and dealers
industries.note: The bill would repeal the federal shield that keeps them off the hook in civil suits for harms from criminal misuse of their products — an immunity no other consumer-product industry has. Its interest in keeping that shield runs against victims who want their day in court.
Repeal would create a new category of civil cases for victims of gun violence, giving plaintiffs' lawyers a new practice area. Their gain depends on victims gaining access to court.
